column1: # effect-boundary-baseline.tsv — XSPEC-383 R8
# Each row is a decision somebody made to NOT fix a zero-effect implementation
# yet. It is not a permission slip; it is a deferral with a clock on it.
# Format: TSV, five tab-separated columns, one row per deferral.
#   family <TAB> member <TAB> verdict <TAB> expires(YYYY-MM-DD) <TAB> reason
# Why TSV and not the JSON the two sibling gates use
# (scripts/reachability-baseline.json, scripts/command-existence-baseline.json):
# XSPEC-383 §7.11.2 specifies TSV-with-per-row-expiry for this gate, the shape
# dev-platform's cross-project/unattended-risks.tsv already uses. The point is
# that the expiry date has to be readable on the same line as the thing it
# governs — in a JSON baseline you unfold three levels before you see the date,
# and a date nobody reads is the same as no date. This is NOT a reason to go
# back and convert the other two.
# Rules the parser enforces (all of them exit 2, not 1 — a broken baseline is
# not "no baseline"):
#   - exactly five tab-separated columns
#   - expires must be YYYY-MM-DD; an entry with no clock never expires, and an
#     exception list with no clock is just a polite delete key
# An expired row exits 1. Expiry does not mean something broke; it means the
# decision to defer needs making again.
# This file is currently EMPTY of rows on purpose. UDS itself declares no effect
# family (it is a standards library plus a CLI — there is no set of interchangeable
# implementations of one effect interface here), so there is nothing to defer.
# The mechanism is exercised by tests/utils/effect-boundary.test.js, not by a
# placeholder row: a fake row would make the file look maintained while proving
# nothing.
# family
